## What you build today

The custom PCB assembled and validated, the flight controller flashed and
talking to the ESC, and the robot flapping in air under wireless control.

## Before you arrive

| | |
|---|---|
| **Parts** | FAAV PCB v3.0, stencil, solder paste, XIAO ESP32S3, JST connectors, battery |
| **Tools** | Hotplate, tweezers, multimeter, bench supply with current limit |
| **Read** | This page and [PCB revisions](/reference/pcb.qmd) |

## Electronic architecture

One 4S (max 16.8 V) battery is connected to a custom PCB that steps VBAT down
to 5 V to power the flight controller. The flight controller generates a 3v3
rail to power the sensors on the custom PCB. Battery power goes through a shunt
for sensing on the custom PCB, then back out to power the ESC. The flight
controller sends commands to the ESC over serial.

## Flight controller

![Microcontroller in its waterproofing box](/Fig/mcu1.jpg){#fig-mcu width=50%}

Firmware lives in [FAAV-Flight-Controller](https://github.com/MIT-AURA-Lab/FAAV-Flight-Controller)
(ESP32, FreeRTOS tasks). See [Software](/reference/software.qmd) for older
variants.

## Assembling the PCB

As of April 2026 the current board is **v3.0**: 4 layers, 21 × 28.5 mm, 34
components. The complete BOM is in the Manufacturing/Assembly folder of the
[FAAV-PCB-v3 repository](https://github.com/MIT-AURA-Lab/FAAV-PCB-v3).

The simplest way to assemble a FAAV PCB is with a stencil, solder paste applied
with a cutter blade, then reflow on the hotplate.

::: {layout-ncol=2}
![Tape blank PCBs around the PCB to assemble](/Fig/PCB_assembly1.jpeg)

![Align the stencil on top and tape it, making sure it sits flat](/Fig/PCB_assembly2.jpeg)
:::

::: {layout-ncol=2}
![Wipe down solder paste with a blade in one firm pass](/Fig/PCB_assembly3.jpeg)

![Place the assembled PCB on the hot plate](/Fig/PCB_assembly4.jpeg)
:::

## Taking the PCB into operation

Once assembled, solder power wires for VBAT and GND at the input side of the
board. Follow these steps **before powering the PCB for the first time**:

1. Check that there is no short circuit between GND and 5V / 3.3V / VBAT.
2. Connect a **15 V supply with a 100 mA current limit** to the battery pads
   and check that it does not draw excessive current.
3. Check with a multimeter that the buck regulator outputs 5 V from the 15 V
   input. The MCU should be on by then.

With the MCU powered, flash your test firmware and check the connection to all
sensors. @tbl-i2c gives the I²C addresses.

| Component | I²C address (bin) | I²C address (hex) |
|---|---|---|
| Pressure sensor | `0b1110110` | `0x76` |
| IMU | `0b1101000` | `0x68` |
| INA228 power monitor | `0b0101000` | `0x40` |

: I²C addresses {#tbl-i2c}

Verify:

- [ ] Voltage, current and temperature readings from the INA228
- [ ] IMU readings
- [ ] Pressure sensor readings
- [ ] RGB LED control

Once all the hardware on the board is validated, solder the power wires at the
output side of the board to the ESC, and the UART wires.

::: {.callout-warning}
## TX to RX

The **TX** output of the PCB has to be connected to the **RX** pin of the ESC,
and vice versa.
:::

## Connectors

The waterproof connector is the JST 8-pin
[08R-JWPF-VSLE-D](https://ch.farnell.com/jst-japan-solderless-terminals/08r-jwpf-vsle-d/connector-housing-rcpt-8pos/dp/2399256)
/ [08T-JWPF-VSLE-D](https://ch.farnell.com/jst-japan-solderless-terminals/08t-jwpf-vsle-d/connector-housing-tab-8pos/dp/2399257).
All pins marked `_b` are used for balancing the battery during recharge. For
use on the robot, connect at least **Vbat** and **GND**; to allow higher
currents, connect **Vbat_b** and **GND_b** as well.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Seal the unused cable slots

Do not forget to seal the back of the connector for the unused cable slots ---
this is a water ingress path straight into the electronics.
:::

![Connector wiring scheme. Left: battery connector. Right: connector on the robot / for recharging the battery.](/Fig/Connector_wiring.png){#fig-connector}
